title: JFK (B): Who was behind the assassination?
question: Who, if anyone, planned or directed the assassination of President Kennedy?

hypotheses.text: Organized crime (Marcello, Trafficante, Giancana), possibly using anti-Castro Cubans
Elements of the CIA, working with anti-Castro Cuban exiles
hypotheses.notes: Course Theses 2 (the CIA) and 4 (Garrison's case against Clay Shaw).

hypotheses.text: Fidel Castro's Cuba, in retaliation for U.S. plots against Castro
U.S. military leaders (LeMay and the Joint Chiefs)
A coalition of establishment, intelligence, military and organized-crime figures acting together ("Rulers of the Realm")
hypotheses.notes: Course Thesis 10 (Sheehan & Billings). The syllabus doesn't spell this thesis out; this wording is inferred from the course's Polinode network ("ROTR Test 4"). Correct it from class notes.

evidence.text: Oswald was a self-professed Marxist who defected to the USSR in 1959 and returned in 1962; documents and testimony show a troubled history, contempt for the U.S. system, violence toward his wife, and an attempt to shoot Gen. Walker.
Despite decades of scrutiny, no money, payments or handlers tying Oswald to any group have been documented; researcher Harold Weisberg said he "never had an extra penny."
Oswald's New Orleans Fair Play for Cuba Committee chapter was a one-man operation using documents he made himself; other leftists kept their distance from him.
Some of Oswald's pro-Castro leaflets were stamped 544 Camp Street, the building that housed former FBI agent Guy Banister's office, a hub of anti-Castro activity.
evidence.notes: Whether Oswald actually worked out of that building is disputed.

evidence.text: The HSCA concluded Oswald was likely seen with David Ferrie, and probably Guy Banister, in Clinton, Louisiana, in late summer 1963.
evidence.notes: Ferrie and Banister were anti-Castro activists; Ferrie also worked for Carlos Marcello's lawyer.

evidence.text: Silvia Odio reported that in late September 1963 three men, one introduced as "Leon Oswald," an ex-Marine, visited her seeking help for anti-Castro activities; the HSCA found her account credible.
evidence.notes: The Warren Commission doubted the timing because Oswald was believed to be traveling to Mexico.

evidence.text: CIA records show Oswald (or someone using his name) contacted Soviet vice consul Valery Kostikov in Mexico City; Kostikov was suspected of belonging to the KGB department responsible for sabotage and assassination.
There are unresolved questions about the Mexico City visit: whether recorded calls were really Oswald, and why CIA reporting at the time omitted details (the HSCA's Lopez Report).

CIA headquarters' October 1963 response about Oswald omitted recent information it had on file (his New Orleans activities); a signer later told researcher John Newman she was signing off on something she knew was not accurate.
The Cuban consulate refused Oswald a visa, and a staffer told him someone like him could only harm the revolution.
On September 7, 1963, Castro publicly warned that U.S. leaders aiding plans to eliminate Cuban leaders would themselves not be safe.
The CIA plotted with Mafia figures Johnny Roselli, Sam Giancana and Santo Trafficante to assassinate Castro (1960–63), as part of a wider covert war against Cuba (Operation Mongoose).
evidence.notes: Gives several groups both motive and capability; also gives Castro a motive.

evidence.text: On the day of the assassination, a CIA officer met Cuban official Rolando Cubela (AMLASH) and offered him a poison device for use against Castro.
The CIA and FBI did not tell the Warren Commission about the plots against Castro; the Church Committee found both agencies' investigations deficient.
evidence.notes: Withholding can protect operations or hide involvement; the inference is the analyst's.

evidence.text: The HSCA concluded the Soviet and Cuban governments, organized crime as a group, and anti-Castro groups as groups were not involved, but could not rule out individual members.
Carlos Marcello allegedly threatened the President in 1962 (the Ed Becker account); the HSCA found Marcello had motive, means and opportunity but no direct evidence of involvement.
evidence.notes: Becker's account is single-sourced and was told years later.

evidence.text: Santo Trafficante allegedly said in 1962 that Kennedy was "going to be hit" (the Jose Aleman account); Aleman qualified his account before the HSCA.
Jack Ruby made phone calls to mob-connected figures in the months before the assassination; testimony links many of them to his dispute with the corruption-ridden variety artists' union (AGVA).
People who knew Ruby, including Dallas police intelligence and his prosecutor, described a volatile, talkative police groupie, not a mob operative; evidence at his trial showed organic brain damage.
Ruby shot Oswald in the Dallas police basement on November 24 during a transfer, ending any chance of a trial; how he got into the basement is disputed.
In June 1964 Ruby begged Earl Warren to take him to Washington so he could tell the truth; Warren declined.
evidence.notes: Ruby's mental state by then is part of the question.

evidence.text: Rose Cheramie, a drug-addicted woman injured on a Louisiana highway, told a state police lieutenant on November 20 that two men she traveled with planned to kill Kennedy in Dallas.
evidence.notes: Single account through the officer, never independently corroborated.

evidence.text: Secret Service agent Abraham Bolden says a plot to shoot the President in Chicago in early November 1963 was reported and handled without written records.
evidence.notes: No records of the plot exist.

evidence.text: Oswald left a note for FBI agent James Hosty at the Dallas office weeks before the assassination; after the assassination it was destroyed on the special agent in charge's order, a fact not revealed until 1975.
evidence.notes: Hosty testified the note complained about visits to his wife; its true content can't be checked.

evidence.text: Allen Dulles, the CIA director Kennedy replaced after the Bay of Pigs, served on the Warren Commission; he was recommended by Robert Kennedy.

Kennedy's relationship with the CIA was repaired after the Bay of Pigs; weeks before his death he publicly defended the agency. The quote about splintering the CIA "into a thousand pieces" is anonymously sourced.
NSAM 263 (October 11, 1963) approved withdrawing 1,000 U.S. advisers from Vietnam by the end of 1963, conditional on progress.
evidence.notes: Read as a planned exit (Syllabus) or as leverage on Diem (Reitzes, quoting Karnow).

evidence.text: In public through November 22, 1963, Kennedy said the U.S. should stay in Vietnam; aides later recalled private talk of withdrawal (O'Donnell, Morse, Forrestal; "Vietnam is not worth another American life").
evidence.notes: Recollections came years later and may be colored by politics (Reitzes p. 9).

evidence.text: In 1962 the Joint Chiefs proposed Operation Northwoods, staged incidents to justify war with Cuba; Kennedy's administration rejected it.
evidence.source: Declassified by the Assassination Records Review Board (1997)
evidence.notes: Shows hostility and willingness at the top of the military, not involvement in 1963.

evidence.text: The claim that Gen. Curtis LeMay ordered the assassination or attended the autopsy is raised in the course but not documented in its materials.
Jim Garrison prosecuted Clay Shaw for conspiracy; the jury acquitted him in March 1969.
Clay Shaw had been a source for the CIA's Domestic Contact Service in the 1950s, something he denied at trial.
evidence.notes: Domestic contacts were common among internationally active businessmen.

evidence.text: E. Howard Hunt, late in life, told his son of a CIA-linked plot (the "Big Event").
evidence.notes: Hunt gave differing accounts at different times.

evidence.text: Years later the KGB forged documents tying Oswald to the CIA as disinformation.
Days before the assassination the Soviet embassy received a crude letter signed "Lee H. Oswald" that seemed to implicate the USSR; Soviet officials treated it as a forgery or provocation.
KGB defector Yuri Nosenko said the KGB took no interest in Oswald and judged him unstable; the CIA confined and questioned Nosenko for years before accepting him as genuine.
After the assassination Soviet propaganda blamed a right-wing cabal; Jacqueline Kennedy lamented that her husband was killed by "some silly little Communist."
Thesis 10's network maps long-running ties among financiers, intelligence officers, military figures and organized-crime and exile operatives.
evidence.notes: Connections show who knew whom, not who did what.

evidence.text: President Johnson pressed the Dallas police to end their investigation and leave it to the FBI.
evidence.notes: Single-sourced in a secondary primer; could reflect a wish to close down rumors of a foreign plot.

evidence.text: Record releases under the 1992 JFK Records Act and by the Review Board (1998) exposed agency secrecy and withheld information but no document showing who, if anyone, directed the assassination.
evidence.notes: Researchers disagree on what the later releases mean.
